query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A data-driven machine-learning interatomic potential, selectively trained on ab initio molecular-dynamics snapshots of both solid and liquid phases at relevant high-temperature conditions, can substantially reduce the computational cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties while retaining fidelity to the underlying ab initio free energies, including vibrational entropy, anharmonic contributions, and electron–vibration coupling.
generation.material_initial_state: A representative multicomponent high-entropy alloy composition (up to five principal elements) in both its solid and molten states near the melting temperature.
generation.intervention: Train a machine-learning potential on systematically chosen ab initio MD configurations spanning solid–liquid transition regimes, ensuring coverage of vibrational and electronic degrees of freedom, and iteratively refine via active learning to accurately capture both phases.
generation.conditions: Temperature range from approximately 0.8 to 1.2 times the melting temperature. Ab initio molecular-dynamics data are derived from density-functional theory calculations at relevant volumes, temperatures, and compositions reflective of the high-entropy system.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical environment representation in the learned potentials, incorporating electron–phonon coupling and anharmonic vibrational contributions from the training data.
generation.mechanism: The machine-learning potential learns the ab initio energy landscape and forces for both crystalline and liquid configurations, enabling accurate and efficient free-energy assessments that incorporate the materials’ high-temperature structural and electronic contributions.
generation.predicted_outcome: This framework will accelerate free-energy evaluations and predict fusion-related thermodynamic properties with near-ab initio accuracy. The expected speedup is at least one order of magnitude compared to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics or TOR-TILD, and maintains a fidelity of a few meV/atom in free energies.
generation.baseline: Full ab initio molecular-dynamics or TOR-TILD workflows that directly compute Gibbs free energies of solid and liquid phases for the same composition and temperature range.
generation.boundary: Demonstration on compositions up to quinary alloys, with measured melting points below 2000–2500 K. Extrapolation to more complex alloys or extreme temperature–pressure regimes requires further validation.
generation.uncertainty: Potential inaccuracies if the ML potential is trained on insufficient or unrepresentative data, or if unanticipated many-body mechanisms dominate at extreme conditions, leading to systematic errors in free-energy predictions.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the ML-derived free energies, melting temperatures, latent heats, and entropies of fusion with those obtained from fully converged ab initio molecular-dynamics or TOR-TILD calculations for the same high-entropy alloy composition across a range of temperatures spanning solid–liquid coexistence.
measurements: Compute free energies, melting temperature, latent heat, and entropy of fusion using ML potentials.
Compute the same thermodynamic quantities using ab initio MD or TOR-TILD reference calculations.
Quantify discrepancies in predicted thermodynamic properties for both solid and liquid phases.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-based approach deviates by more than an agreed-upon threshold (e.g., >5 meV/atom in free energy or >2% in derived thermodynamic properties) compared to ab initio or TOR-TILD references, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe ability to predict and understand phases in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) is still being debated, and primarily true predictive capabilities derive from the known thermodynamics of materials. The present work demonstrates that prior work using high-throughput first-principles calculations may be further utilized to provide direct insight into the temperature- and composition-dependent phase evolution in HEAs, particularly Al-containing HEAs with a strengthening multiphase microstructure. Using a simple model with parameters derived from first-principles calculations, we reproduce the major features associated with Al-containing phases, demonstrating a generalizable approach for exploring potential phase evolution where little experimental data exists. Neutron scattering, in situ microscopy, and calorimetry measurements suggest that our high-throughput Monte Carlo technique captures both qualitative and quantitative features for both intermetallic phase formation and microstructure evolution at lower temperatures. In this section, we discuss the results of the development of the interatomic-potential model used to enable the application of MD simulations of dislocation properties in bcc MoNbTaW. We employ the general framework of machine-learning (ML)-based approaches, which have emerged recently as a systematic framework to develop potentials with accuracies near that of the underlying DFT calculations for elemental and multicomponent systems,. Here, using training data reported previously for elemental, binary, ternary, and quaternary systems in Nb–Ta–Mo–W, we developed a potential for the MoNbTaW RHEA based on the moment tensor potential (MTP) formalism, which has been found to feature an excellent balance between accuracy and computational cost. The flowchart for constructing the MTP is shown in Fig. 1a with the methodological details provided in “Methods”. The basic materials property predictions of the MTP model are provided in Supplementary Table 1. decision.trend: Following early efforts to predict phase stability in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) primarily by focusing on electronic structure and phase diagrams, researchers introduced computational workflows coupling first-principles methods with high-throughput or machine-learning frameworks. Paper PMC6207727 demonstrated how simple models trained on first-principles inputs successfully predicted phase evolution across a high temperature range for Al-containing HEAs. Paper PMC6820750 corroborated that data-driven approaches leveraging binary phase diagrams can reduce the reliance on brute-force ab initio methods. Most recently, Paper PMC11275555 presents a scheme to integrate advanced ab initio and Bayesian optimization, indicating steady progress toward minimal data, high-accuracy predictive methods for multicomponent alloys. However, none of these studies fully addresses the combined requirement of accurately capturing vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling for both solid and liquid phases at high temperatures in a way that drastically lowers computational cost.
decision.unsolved: Despite the use of machine learning potentials and advanced sampling, a cost-effective method to compute fully converged free energies (including vibrational and electronic contributions) for both solid and liquid states in complex multi-principal-element alloys remains elusive. Existing approaches either sacrifice accuracy by relying on empirical potentials or remain prohibitively expensive when using fully ab initio molecular dynamics, especially for high-entropy compositions.
decision.lever: Develop a machine-learning interatomic potential trained on selective ab initio molecular-dynamics data for both solid and molten configurations, capturing vibrational and electronic degrees of freedom. Key parameters include uniform sampling of high-temperature structural configurations, explicit electron–phonon coupling in the training data, and iterative model refinement with active learning to ensure coverage of liquid–solid transitions.
decision.why: This approach emerges from increasing reliance on machine-learning potentials to reproduce ab initio–level accuracy without the prohibitive cost of large-scale first-principles molecular dynamics. The referenced work in developing computationally affordable yet reliable methods highlights the efficiency gains from data-driven strategies (PMC6207727, PMC6820750), while the advanced multi-objective frameworks (PMC11275555) show that a small but carefully designed training set of ab initio data can yield models with fidelity to both phases. The decisive benchmark will be comparing the ML-derived free energies and corresponding fusion properties (latent heat, entropy of fusion, melting temperatures) against full ab initio molecular-dynamics and TOR-TILD results for a well-characterized high-entropy alloy composition in both solid and liquid states.
